item.title: Writing for Dark Times — Tue Oct 6, 11:45 AM — Smith Warehouse
item.description:
Duke English and the Franklin Humanities Institute will host a talk by Hadji Bakara, Associate Professor of English at the University of Michigan. Bakara will explain how writing has shaped the history and ideas of human rights. While writers have helped highlight human rights, scholars and the public mostly see literature as a way to show when human rights are broken. This means people understand human rights by noticing when they are missing.
Writers themselves thought differently. Looking at the lives and work of writers like B. Traven, Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'O, Agostinho Neto, Nadine Gordimer, Archibald MacLeish, Seamus Heaney, Muriel Rukeyser, Czesław Miłosz, and Toni Morrison, Bakara shows that writers who faced the loss of human rights frequently asked questions about their own work: What is writing? item.title: Best Friend or Cybermother? A Confucian Reflection on AI Companionship — Tue Oct 6, 12:00 PM — Rubenstein Library Carpenter Conference Room 249
item.description:
AI companions designed to simulate romantic or friendly intimacy are rapidly expanding, but most critiques remain framed by Western liberal assumptions. I develop an alternative critique grounded in Confucian ethics. It begins by challenging the industry claim that AI companions offer a remedy for loneliness.
Against this view, I argue that Confucianism values positive solitude as a condition of self-cultivation and a precondition for genuine friendship. I further argue that AI companions are better understood as cyber mothers, inviting dependency and regression rather than ethical development. On this basis, I also criticize Nobel prize winner Geoffrey Hinton's proposal that future AGI should be designed to exhibit maternal love.

item.title: Learning in Networks Reading Group — Tue Oct 6, 12:00 PM — Gross Hall
item.description:
Learning in Networks Reading Group and Seminar Series: Tuesdays, 12pm in 330 Gross Hall; lunch included The institute focuses on fundamental questions in statistical inference, machine learning, causal inference, and optimization on networks, with particular emphasis on statistical-computational tradeoffs, message-passing algorithms, learning dynamics, and network-based market design. By fostering collaboration across disciplines, the institute aims to develop new mathematical and algorithmic foundations for understanding complex networked systems and their applications. The institute is led by collaborators Jiaming Xu, Alex Belloni, Fan Wei, Galen Reeves, and James Moody. Learn more: https://sites.duke.edu/learninginnetworks/
Source: Duke University

item.title: Novel Justice: Pink Crime with Valena Beety — Tue Oct 6, 12:30 PM — Law School 4055
item.description:
Join Valena Beety, Robert H. McKinney Professor of Law at Indiana University Bloomington, for a discussion of her new book, Pink Crime.
An innocence litigator and former federal prosecutor, Professor Beety examines how prosecutorial overreach, flawed forensic science, and cultural panic intersect in the criminalization of motherhood, pregnancy, and queer identity. She also explores how recent changes in law and policy have expanded the reach of the criminal legal system.
Lunch will be provided.
Sponsored by the Wilson Center for Science and Justice and Duke Law's OutLaw.
Source: Duke University

item.title: Structure, Function, and Evolution of Gene Regulatory Networks in Extreme Stress Response — Tue Oct 6, 12:30 PM — Nanaline Duke 147
item.description:
Research in my lab seeks to elucidate how cells make decisions in response to environmental cues. My particular focus is on how networks of molecules interact within free-living microbial cells. These networks govern the decision to grow when conditions are optimal or deploy damage repair systems when faced with stress. I study microbial stress responses in extremophiles of the domainArchaea, which represent extreme examples of microbes surviving damage by multiple stressors.
Source: Duke University

item.title: Building Agents in ChatGPT — Tue Oct 6, 1:00 PM — The TEC - Technology Engagement Center
item.description:
Learn to build AI assistants that work for you. This hands-on workshop introduces ChatGPT Workspace Agents - AI that can run multi-step workflows on a schedule, connect to Outlook and SharePoint, and create and share files.
You'll start with Agent Skills: reusable packages of instructions and examples that shape how an agent behaves. You'll build your own personalized "communication style" skill from your real writing samples, learning a technique that transfers to any task where you want AI to match a style or follow a procedure.
Then you'll build a working personal assistant agent from scratch - describing it in plain language, refining it with the builder agent, attaching skills, testing it on a real weekly work review, scheduling it to run automatically, and sharing it with colleagues.
Come with a task you'd like to hand off. Leave with an agent that does it
Source: Duke University

item.title: 🎤 Karaoke Night at The Tavern 🍻 — Sat Oct 17, 8:45 PM
item.description:
Discover Durham Together Looking for an actually fun night out in Durham? This is one of those spots where the whole place just clicks.
Huge bar. Pool tables. Darts. A full karaoke stage. And a crowd that’s there to have a good time — whether you’re singing, cheering people on, or just hanging with friends over drinks.
The karaoke here is genuinely awesome because people actually get into it. You’ll hear everything from pop punk and country to throwback rap, emo classics, rock anthems, and songs everyone ends up singing together by the end of the night.
No pressure to perform. No “serious singer” vibe. Just good energy, great people, and one of the most entertaining nights you can have in Durham.
Come solo, bring friends, grab a drink, play some pool, put your name on the list, or just enjoy the show. Either way, you’ll probably leave with a sore voice and a few new friends. 🎶
Source: Meetup: Discover Durham Together

item.title: Schenck Forest & Umstead Loop — Sun Nov 15, 1:00 PM — Carl Alwin Schenck Memorial Forest
item.description:
Join TLC on this special partner hike through Schenck Forest and Umstead State Park! Naturalist and TLC Trail guide, Julie Hall, will guide you on this 5-mile hike through Schenck Forest and a short section of the City of Raleigh Greenway to reach the Walton Farm. Mary Walton is looking forward to speaking with the group about the Conservation Easement process and working with TLC on this partnership to protect her farm. We will get to walk through a portion of the farm, and then head back on the greenway and through Schenk Forest to complete a loop.
This is a free event, but preregistration is required. Schenck Forest serves as a working forest and outdoor laboratory for North Carolina State University students, so there is a strict no dog policy.
Source: Triangle Land Conservancy

item.title: Biomimicry: Nature as a Mentor — Tue Nov 17, 9:30 AM — Swift Creek Bluffs Nature Preserve
item.description:
Learn about biomimicry at Swift Creek Bluffs! Biomimicry (from the Greek bios, meaning life, and mimesis, meaning to imitate) is the practice of looking at how plants, animals, and ecosystems solve problems and then copying those designs to solve human challenges. It’s not about using nature as a resource (like cutting down trees for wood); it’s about learning from nature as a mentor.
Join Hike Leader, Leigh Aultman, for a morning of Biological Storytelling. We will walk the short creek loop trail with up to six stops where stories will be shared about local organisms' biological adaptations and how those adaptations and innovations can inform human designs. This is a free event, but preregistration is required. Due to the size of the parking lot, we will keep the hiking group small and ask that you register by vehicle rather than individual. Feel free to bring guests but please carpool to ensure we have enough space in the parking lot.
Source: Triangle Land Conservancy
